entries.question: Who wrote the (second set of) ten commandments?
entries.summary: Exodus 34:1 has YHWH explicitly saying "I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables." Deuteronomy 10:4 confirms "he wrote on the tables" — God did it. But Exodus 34:27-28 says "the LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words ... And he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments." The subject of "he wrote" in 34:28 is most naturally Moses. So within four verses of Exodus 34, God and Moses are both described as writing the tablets.
entries.commentary:
The apologist response focuses entirely on the ambiguous pronoun in 34:28 — who is the antecedent of "he wrote"? Archer, Stuart, and Sarna all argue that "he" in 34:28 refers back to YHWH from 34:27 ("the LORD said"), not to Moses. On this reading 34:27 commands Moses to write something (the covenant stipulations for Israel, not the tablets), and 34:28 describes YHWH writing the Decalogue on the tablets. The Hebrew is ambiguous enough to allow this parsing.

This is not a ridiculous reading. The Hebrew pronoun is underdetermined and Deuteronomy 10:4 clearly attributes the writing to God. The harmonization is not desperate. But the more natural reading of 34:27-28 in sequence has Moses as the subject throughout: "The LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words: for after the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel. And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water. And he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments." Moses is the one who was with YHWH, did not eat or drink, and wrote. The natural grammatical subject is Moses.

The critical explanation is straightforward. Exodus 34 preserves an older tradition — often identified with J or a J/E composite — where Moses himself inscribes the tablets, which contained what is sometimes called the "Ritual Decalogue" (Exod 34:14-26) rather than the Ethical Decalogue of Exodus 20 and Deut 5. Goethe was already noticing this in the 18th century, and Wellhausen made it standard. The Priestly and Deuteronomistic traditions then asserted divine authorship of the tablets (Exod 24:12, 31:18, 32:15-16, Deut 10:1-5), partially overwriting the older Mosaic-authorship tradition. Exodus 34 as we have it shows both claims sitting uneasily together.

William Propp in his Anchor Bible commentary argues 34:27-28 preserves an older source where Moses carved the tablets himself. Dozeman agrees. Even conservative scholars like Sarna acknowledge the ambiguity requires interpretation. Verdict: the pronoun-reference harmonization is grammatically available but strains against the narrative flow. The source-critical explanation accounts for both the ambiguity and the Priestly override.

commentary_out.commentary:
Within a few verses Exodus 34 names two different writers of the second set of tablets. Exodus 34:1 has YHWH announce, in the first person, 'I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables,' and Deuteronomy 10:2, 10:4 confirm divine authorship: 'he wrote on the tables, according to the first writing.' But Exodus 34:27-28 reads: 'the LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words... And he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.' In the natural flow of v. 28 the subject of 'he wrote' is Moses — the same Moses who in that verse 'was there with the LORD forty days,' ate no bread, and drank no water.

The apologetic case, advanced by Archer and (more cautiously) by Sarna and Stuart, hinges on the ambiguous antecedent of 'he wrote' in 34:28. They argue the subject reverts to YHWH from 34:27a ('the LORD said'): v. 27 commands Moses to write the surrounding covenant stipulations, while v. 28 reports YHWH writing the Decalogue itself onto the stone — matching 34:1 and Deuteronomy 10:4. Hebrew narrative pronouns are frequently underdetermined, and the strong claim of Deuteronomy 10:4 gives the reading external support, so it is not desperate. It should be noted that not all conservative commentators take this line: John Durham's WBC volume, for instance, reads Moses as the writer in 34:28, which shows that even within the traditional camp the pronoun is not uniformly resolved in YHWH's favor.

The grammar leans toward Moses without being decisive. Both Exodus 34:1 (YHWH writing) and 34:28 (the disputed clause, wayyiktov) are plain qal active forms with explicit subject-object syntax; neither uses a causative hiphil that would mean 'caused to be written.' The absence of a hiphil is not itself proof, however, since Hebrew narrative routinely shifts to an unmarked new subject without any morphological flag — the antecedent question is contextual, not morphological. On the contextual reading, the nearest and most natural subject in v. 28 is Moses, the continuous actor of the clause sequence (he was there; he ate not; he drank not; he wrote). To make YHWH the subject one must reach back over Moses to v. 27a, against the narrative momentum. Sarna's JPS commentary candidly registers the ambiguity rather than resolving it cleanly.

The sharper observation is what 'these words' in 34:27 actually denotes. The covenant content of Exodus 34:11-26 — often called the Ritual or Cultic Decalogue (festivals, firstlings, no leavened bread with blood, the boiling-a-kid prohibition) — differs markedly from the Ethical Decalogue of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5. Yet 34:28 calls what is written 'the ten commandments' (literally 'the ten words,' aseret ha-devarim). Goethe already flagged this discrepancy in the 18th century (in his 1773 essay distinguishing the Decalogue of Exodus 34 from that of Exodus 20), and Wellhausen made it a standard datum: Exodus 34 likely preserves an older, independent covenant document in which Moses himself inscribed the tablets, later harmonized to the Sinai Decalogue tradition.

The broader redactional picture is consistent. A cluster of texts assert divine authorship of the tablets — Exodus 24:12, 31:18 ('written with the finger of God'), 32:15-16 ('the writing was the writing of God'), and Deuteronomy 10:1-5 — reflecting the Priestly and Deuteronomistic interest in the tablets as a direct divine artifact. Exodus 34:27-28, on the older reading defended by Propp and Dozeman, preserves a Mosaic-authorship notice from a J/E-related stratum that the divine-authorship framing only partially overwrote. The result is a text that, read straight, has both God (34:1) and Moses (34:28) inscribe the same stones. Friedman's source-divided text assigns the divine-authorship notices and the Mosaic-authorship notice to different hands, accounting for the seam.

Verdict: partially harmonizable. The pronoun-antecedent reading is grammatically available and is reinforced by Deuteronomy 10:4, so a reader committed to harmony can land on divine authorship throughout; but it strains the syntax of v. 28 and ignores the Ritual-Decalogue problem. Source criticism explains both the ambiguity and the conflicting claims as the seam between an older Mosaic-authorship tradition and the dominant divine-authorship tradition.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The pronoun 'he wrote' in Exodus 34:28 can grammatically refer back to YHWH (34:27a), and Deuteronomy 10:4 explicitly attributes the writing to God, so divine authorship can be read throughout; this resolution strains the natural syntax of v. 28 (where Moses is the continuous subject) and leaves the Ritual-Decalogue content of 34:11-26 unaccounted for, which source criticism attributes to an older Mosaic-authorship stratum overlaid by the divine-authorship tradition.

issues.problem: The commentary attributes to Goethe a '1773 essay distinguishing the Decalogue of Exodus 34 from that of Exodus 20.' Goethe's relevant work is 'Zwo wichtige bisher unerörterte biblische Fragen' (Two Important Biblical Questions Hitherto Undiscussed), published in 1773, in which he argued the tablets contained the cultic commands of Exodus 34 (the so-called 'Ritual Decalogue'). The dating and substance are essentially correct, but the precise claim that Goethe 'distinguished' the two decalogues is a slight over-precision of a more general argument about which commands stood on the tablets. Low-to-medium confidence; the attribution is broadly defensible but should be stated more cautiously.
issues.correction: Soften to: 'Goethe already raised the question of the tablets' content in his 1773 essay,' rather than crediting him with the modern Ritual/Ethical Decalogue distinction in its developed form.

entries.question: Is God merciful?
entries.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalms, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Joel, Micah, Judith, 2 Corinthians, James, 1 John
entries.summary: Dozens of texts describe YHWH as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in loyalty — Exodus 34:6, Deut 4:31, the Psalms, the prophets, the New Testament letters. SAB cites Exodus 34:6-7 for the opposite claim, since the full formula in 34:7 adds that God visits the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation. The classic mercy-formula is itself the source of both sides of this contradiction.
entries.commentary:
The SAB framing here is actually too weak. Exodus 34:6-7 is not "God is cruel, unmerciful, and evil." The full text is: "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation." The apologist is correct that this is not a contradiction between mercy-texts and a cruelty-text — it is a single text that holds mercy and justice together.

That said, there is a real contradiction in the wider biblical tradition that SAB has imperfectly gestured at. Ezekiel 18 explicitly reverses the transgenerational punishment doctrine: "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son." Deuteronomy 24:16 similarly forbids judicial punishment of children for fathers' sins. But Exodus 20:5, 34:7, Numbers 14:18, Deuteronomy 5:9, and 2 Samuel 21 (where YHWH kills seven of Saul's descendants for Saul's treaty-breaking) all operate on transgenerational liability. That is a real intra-biblical tension.

Second, the "merciful" texts themselves sit alongside texts where YHWH commands the extermination of entire populations including infants (1 Sam 15:3), drowns the world minus Noah's family, sends plagues killing firstborns, orders Jericho's total destruction. The apologist harmonization — Copan, Flannagan, Blomberg — argues that divine mercy operates within a just framework where judgment is warranted, so none of these actions are incompatible with mercy. The problem is that "merciful, but also willing to command the killing of infants" is stretching the ordinary meaning of merciful pretty thin.

Yehezkel Kaufmann and more recently Joel Kaminsky have done careful work on the transgenerational issue, arguing that ancient Israelite religion operated with a corporate personality concept where the individual-family-tribe-nation was a spiritual continuum. That is the cultural context. But Ezekiel 18 is explicitly repudiating that framework, which is itself evidence of an intra-biblical theological development. Verdict: SAB's framing is imprecise — Exodus 34:6-7 is not the right proof-text for divine cruelty. But the underlying tension between the mercy formula and the transgenerational punishment doctrine, and between mercy and herem warfare, is real and well-documented in critical scholarship.

answers.answer: God is cruel, unmerciful, and evil.
answers.answer_explanation: The Lord God ... visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation. Exodus 34:6-7

commentary_out.commentary:
The proof-text the Skeptic's Annotated Bible deploys is poorly chosen, and saying so is part of an honest analysis. Exodus 34:6-7 is a single, balanced formula — the grace formula (Gnadenformel) — not two opposed verses. It reads: 'merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children... unto the third and to the fourth generation.' Mercy and retributive justice are deliberately held together in one breath; the abundant clauses on mercy outweigh the brief retributive coda. As a stand-alone case for 'God is cruel,' the citation fails, and Moberly, Sarna, and Scoralick all read 34:6-7 as a unified affirmation of patient grace. The dozens of parallel texts (Deut 4:31; Pss 86:5; 103:8; 145:9; Joel 2:13; Micah 7:18) simply echo this same formula.

There are, however, two real intra-biblical tensions the SAB has only imperfectly gestured toward. The first is transgenerational liability. Exodus 20:5, 34:7, Numbers 14:18, and Deuteronomy 5:9 all affirm that YHWH visits the fathers' iniquity on children to the third and fourth generation, and 2 Samuel 21 enacts it: 2 Samuel 21:1 traces a three-year famine to 'Saul, and his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites' — that is, to Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites in violation of Israel's earlier sworn covenant to spare them (the treaty narrated in Joshua 9; the link to Joshua 9 is the standard scholarly identification, not a citation within 2 Samuel 21 itself). Seven of Saul's descendants are then handed over to the Gibeonites and executed to expiate the bloodguilt. Against this, Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids precisely such judicial transfer ('the fathers shall not be put to death for the children'), and Ezekiel 18 issues a sustained, programmatic repudiation: 'The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father... the soul that sinneth, it shall die.' Jeremiah 31:29-30 likewise overturns the sour-grapes proverb. This is a genuine theological development — and Ezekiel's emphatic correction is itself evidence that the older corporate model was felt to be a live, problematic doctrine, not a settled harmony.

The critical scholarship reads this through the lens of corporate personality and its later individualization. Joel Kaminsky's *Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible* and the older synthesis of Yehezkel Kaufmann describe an early Israelite framework in which the family, clan, and nation formed a moral continuum, so that guilt and its consequences could traverse generations. Ezekiel 18, written in the exile when that corporate logic had become unbearable ('our fathers have sinned... and we have borne their iniquities,' Lam 5:7), recasts responsibility as strictly individual. The canon preserves both stages without reconciling them; the transgenerational formula stands in Exodus and Numbers, the individual-retribution doctrine in Ezekiel and Deuteronomy 24. Moshe Weinfeld locates the Deuteronomic individual-retribution principle within the broader humanizing tendency of the Deuteronomic law.

The second tension is between the mercy formula and the texts in which YHWH commands or executes mass killing — the herem of 1 Samuel 15:3 ('slay both man and woman, infant and suckling'), the flood, the death of Egypt's firstborn, the total destruction of Jericho. The apologetic response of Copan and Flannagan is that divine mercy operates within a framework of just judgment: where judgment is deserved, executing it is not incompatible with being merciful, and some herem language is itself hyperbolic. That argument has force against caricature, and the hyperbole point is real for parts of Joshua. But it stretches the ordinary semantic range of 'merciful, slow to anger' to include the commanded killing of infants, and it cannot absorb the explicit reversal in Ezekiel 18.

Verdict: the SAB framing is overstated — Exodus 34:6-7 is not a cruelty proof-text but a unified formula. The genuine and well-documented tension lies elsewhere: between the transgenerational-punishment doctrine of Exodus/Numbers/Deuteronomy 5 (and 2 Samuel 21) and its explicit repudiation in Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24:16, a tension best understood as theological development from corporate to individual retribution rather than a flat logical contradiction within one stratum.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The cited proof-text, Exodus 34:6-7, is a single unified formula holding mercy and justice together, so it does not pit a mercy-text against a cruelty-text; the real and unresolved tension is the genuinely contradictory transgenerational-punishment doctrine (Exod 20:5; 34:7; Num 14:18; Deut 5:9; 2 Sam 21) against its explicit reversal in Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24:16, best explained as a development from corporate to individual retribution rather than as logically reconcilable within one stratum.

entries.question: Who may offer sacrifices to God?
entries.summary: The Priestly legislation in Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 restricts sacrifice to Aaronide priests at the tabernacle door, threatening death for any layperson who slaughters away from that one altar. But 1 Samuel happily reports Samuel — an Ephraimite, not a Levite — offering a burnt offering at Mizpah, and YHWH answers him without complaint.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization runs through Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties and Walter Kaiser's Hard Sayings. Their move is to argue that Samuel was a special case — a divinely commissioned prophet operating before the centralization at Jerusalem, that 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 retroactively makes Samuel a Levite by reckoning his line through Kohath, and that pre-temple sacrifice at high places was tolerated until Solomon's temple was built. Plenty of patriarchs offered sacrifices, the argument goes, so Samuel is just continuing that pattern in an unsettled period.

This harmonization has real exegetical weight on the high-places point. The Deuteronomistic Historian repeatedly notes that high-place sacrifice was tolerated "because the temple was not yet built" (1 Kings 3:2), and the genealogical retrojection in Chronicles is a known phenomenon. The problem is that the Numbers and Leviticus texts don't say "after the temple is built." Numbers 18:7 says any "stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death," and Leviticus 17:3-4 says any Israelite who slaughters in the camp or out of the camp without bringing it to the tabernacle door has "shed blood" and shall be "cut off from among his people." That's an unconditional death penalty, not a temporary measure.

The critical-scholarly read recognizes this as a classic source-critical fault line. Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 are Priestly material (P/H), reflecting a post-exilic ideology of cultic centralization with the Aaronide priesthood at the top. The Samuel narrative is older Deuteronomistic material that pre-dates that ideology and assumes a much more decentralized cult. Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena laid this out in 1878, and Israel Knohl's The Sanctuary of Silence has refined the dating but kept the basic insight: the Priestly source is projecting its own cultic vision back into Mosaic times. Samuel isn't violating the law — he's operating in a literary world where that law hasn't been imagined yet.

The Chronicler's Levite-Samuel move is itself good evidence that the post-exilic editors saw the problem and tried to paper over it. That is of course a subjective read of the editorial intent, but the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6 is hard to reconcile with the Ephraimite framing of 1 Samuel 1:1, which is the older text. Verdict: genuine contradiction, driven by competing source traditions about who could legitimately approach the altar.

commentary_out.commentary:
The two answer-streams in this entry sit on opposite sides of one of the oldest recognized fault lines in Pentateuchal source criticism. The Priestly legislation draws the cult to a single point and a single family: Numbers 18:7 grants the 'priest's office' to Aaron and his sons 'as a service of gift,' and adds that 'the stranger (zar) that cometh nigh shall be put to death.' Leviticus 17:3-4 (part of the Holiness Code, H) extends the principle to ordinary slaughter — any Israelite who kills an ox, lamb, or goat in or out of the camp without bringing it to 'the door of the tabernacle' has 'shed blood' and is 'cut off (karet) from among his people.' Against this stands 1 Samuel 7:9, where Samuel — introduced in 1 Samuel 1:1 as the son of Elkanah 'an Ephrathite' (ephrati) of the hill country of Ephraim — 'took a sucking lamb, and offered it for a burnt offering wholly unto the LORD,' at Mizpah, far from any central sanctuary, and 'the LORD heard him.' The narrative records neither rebuke nor death; it records answered prayer. (The contradiction depends on Samuel being a non-Levite. The source answer's parenthetical gloss of 'Ephrathite' as 'a member of the tribe of Judah' is itself mistaken: ephrati in 1 Samuel 1:1 means Ephraimite, as the immediate context — Ramathaim-zophim of Mount Ephraim — confirms; the same term means Bethlehemite-Judahite elsewhere, e.g. 1 Sam 17:12, but not here. Either way Samuel is not an Aaronide.)

The strongest apologetic harmonization, developed by Gleason Archer in his *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* and by the contributors to *Hard Sayings of the Bible*, has three moving parts. First, Samuel was a divinely commissioned prophet operating in an unsettled premonarchic period before any central altar existed; the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) sacrificed freely, and Samuel continues that pattern. Second, 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 (MT 6:18-23) reckons Samuel's line through Kohath, making him a Levite after all, so he is not strictly a 'stranger.' Third, the Deuteronomistic Historian himself concedes that high-place sacrifice was tolerated 'because there was no house built unto the name of the LORD' (1 Kings 3:2), so the centralization restriction simply was not yet in force.

The high-place point carries genuine exegetical weight — the bamot were demonstrably in legitimate use throughout the premonarchic and early monarchic periods (Samuel at Mizpah and Ramah, Elijah at Carmel, Solomon at Gibeon), and the Deuteronomistic narrator does not condemn them before the temple. The genealogical retrojection in Chronicles is likewise a recognized phenomenon. But the harmonization founders on what the Priestly texts actually say, and it is worth being precise about why the conceded force of the bamot point does not rescue it. The toleration of high places is a Deuteronomistic datum drawn from the book of Kings; it is a concession internal to that corpus's own theology of centralization-once-the-temple-exists. The Priestly and Holiness laws in Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 operate on entirely different premises and attach no temporal qualifier. They do not say 'until the temple is built'; Leviticus 17:7 grounds the rule in a permanent statute 'throughout their generations,' and the penalties — death for the encroaching layman, karet for the unauthorized slaughterer — are framed as unconditional and immediate. One cannot import the Deuteronomistic loophole into the Priestly law that explicitly excludes it; the two corpora simply do not share the assumption that local sacrifice was ever legitimate. That is precisely why the harmonization that works within the Deuteronomistic History does not bridge to the Priestly material — and why the verdict is non-harmonization rather than partial harmonization.

Critical scholarship reads this as a textbook source seam. Numbers 18 and Leviticus 17 are Priestly/Holiness material reflecting a centralizing cultic ideology with the Aaronide priesthood at its apex; the Samuel narratives are older traditions embedded in the Deuteronomistic History that presuppose a decentralized cult with sacrifice at many local sites. Julius Wellhausen's *Prolegomena* set out the basic developmental scheme, in which P's centralization is a late projection backward; Israel Knohl's *The Sanctuary of Silence* refined the relative dating of P and H without overturning the core insight that the Priestly vision projects later cultic centralization back into the Mosaic age. P. Kyle McCarter's Anchor Bible *I Samuel* treats Samuel's Mizpah offering as wholly unremarkable within its own narrative world — precisely because that world has not yet imagined the Aaronide monopoly. Jacob Milgrom's and Baruch Levine's Anchor Bible volumes on Leviticus and Numbers locate the encroachment-and-slaughter statutes squarely within the Priestly system, treating the death penalty for lay encroachment as constitutive of P's theology of graded holiness.

The Chronicler's move is itself the best evidence that ancient editors felt the problem. By relocating Samuel into a Levitical genealogy, 1 Chronicles 6 quietly resolves the difficulty the older Ephraimite framing of 1 Samuel 1:1 creates — but the two cannot both be the original datum, and the Ephraimite notice is the earlier text. Reading editorial intent always carries some subjectivity, yet the direction of harmonization (lay Ephraimite becomes Levite) points one way and reflects a postexilic anxiety to fit Samuel's recognized cultic role into the now-canonical Aaronide-Levitical system. The tension is not dissolved by appeal to prophetic exception, because the Priestly law admits no such exception.

Verdict: genuine contradiction, generated by competing source traditions over who could legitimately approach the altar.

entries.question: How many male Levites more than one month old did Moses and Aaron count?
entries.summary: Numbers 3:39 gives the total of all male Levites a month old and upward as 22,000. But the same chapter breaks the count into clans — 7,500 Gershonites (3:22), 8,600 Kohathites (3:28), and 6,200 Merarites (3:34) — which sums to 22,300, not 22,000. The 300-Levite gap is internal to a single chapter.
entries.commentary:
This is a genuine arithmetic problem internal to Numbers 3, and the apologetic harmonization tradition has been working it for centuries. The standard move from Keil and Delitzsch onward, picked up by Gleason Archer and Timothy Ashley in NICOT Numbers, is the firstborn-deduction theory. Numbers 3:40-51 has YHWH command Moses to use the Levites as a substitution for the firstborn of all Israel, and there are 22,273 firstborn Israelites (3:43). The deal is one Levite per firstborn, with a 5-shekel redemption fee for the surplus 273 firstborn. For that exchange to work, the apologetic argument runs, the 300 Levites in question must themselves be firstborn — they can't redeem someone else's firstborn status because they already have their own. So the round 22,000 number in 3:39 represents Levites available for substitution, with 300 firstborn Levites excluded from that count.

This explanation has the virtue of using the immediate context to solve the problem, and it's not crazy. Numbers 3:40-51 is clearly thinking about firstborn-Levite substitution and a 273-firstborn surplus does need to be redeemed somehow. But the explanation has two significant problems. First, the text doesn't say this. Numbers 3:39 says "all that were numbered of the Levites... were twenty and two thousand," which on a plain reading is the total count, not a substitution-eligible subset. The harmonization requires reading an unstated qualification into the verse. Second, the 300-firstborn-Levites number is itself stipulated to make the math work — there's no independent textual evidence that exactly 300 Levite firstborn existed.

More importantly, the critical-scholarly take recognizes this as one of many internal numerical inconsistencies that betray Numbers' compositional history. Baruch Levine and Jacob Milgrom both note that the Priestly census materials contain numbers that don't always reconcile, suggesting either scribal corruption in transmission (textual critics like Emanuel Tov flag exactly this kind of round-number/sum mismatch as common) or layered redaction where the clan figures and the round total come from different sources. The Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch both preserve the same numbers, so the corruption (if that's what it is) is pre-LXX.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The firstborn-Levites apologetic move is clever and contextually motivated, but it's an unstated qualification read into 3:39 specifically to save the math. The simpler explanation is that Numbers 3 contains an arithmetic problem the redactors either didn't notice or didn't care about — which itself tells you something about how the text was transmitted.
entries.scholarship: Baruch A. Levine, *Numbers 1-20*, Anchor Bible 4 (Doubleday, 1993). Jacob Milgrom, *Numbers*, JPS Torah Commentary (Jewish Publication Society, 1990). Timothy R. Ashley, *The Book of Numbers*, NICOT (Eerdmans, 1993). Philip J. Budd, *Numbers*, Word Biblical Commentary 5 (Word, 1984). Emanuel Tov, *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012). Carl Friedrich Keil and Franz Delitzsch, *Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: Pentateuch* (T&T Clark, 1864-1892). Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

commentary_out.commentary:
Numbers 3:39 gives the total of all Levite males a month old and upward as 22,000. The clan subtotals in the same chapter — 7,500 Gershonites (3:22), 8,600 Kohathites (3:28), and 6,200 Merarites (3:34) — sum to 22,300 in the Masoretic Text. The 300-Levite discrepancy is internal to a single chapter and turns on simple addition.

The long-running apologetic harmonization is the firstborn-deduction theory, traceable to Keil and Delitzsch and carried forward by Gleason Archer and (cautiously) Timothy Ashley in NICOT *Numbers*. Its premise is the substitution scheme of 3:40-51: the Levites are taken in place of the firstborn of Israel, with 22,273 Israelite firstborn counted (3:43) and a 273-firstborn surplus redeemed at five shekels each (3:46-48). The argument runs that the 300 'missing' Levites are themselves *firstborn*, and a firstborn Levite cannot stand in for another firstborn — he already bears his own consecrated status — so the 22,000 figure in 3:39 is not the gross total but the count of Levites *available for substitution*, with 300 firstborn Levites set aside. This has the genuine virtue of solving the problem from the chapter's own logic, and the substitution arithmetic of 3:43-48 really does require careful bookkeeping of firstborn.

But the harmonization carries two weaknesses. First, the text does not say it. Numbers 3:39 reads, 'all that were numbered of the Levites... were twenty and two thousand' — *kol-pequdei ha-leviyyim*, an unqualified total. To read it as a substitution-eligible subset is to import a restriction the verse does not state. Second, the figure of 300 firstborn Levites is reverse-engineered to balance the sum; there is no independent attestation of that number anywhere in the chapter, and the redemption transaction in 3:40-51 concerns the surplus of *Israelite* firstborn over *all* Levites, not over a reduced count. The harmonization rescues the arithmetic at the cost of inventing a datum.

The text-critical reading is more economical. A commonly proposed scholarly explanation is a numeral corruption in the Kohathite total: where the MT of 3:28 reads 8,600, a number of commentators conjecture an original 8,300. With 8,300 Kohathites, the three subtotals (7,500 + 8,300 + 6,200) sum to exactly 22,000 — matching the grand total in 3:39. It must be stated precisely what kind of evidence this is. This 8,300 figure is a conjectural emendation proposed to harmonize the sum, not a securely attested reading of the Septuagint; the standard LXX (Rahlfs and the major uncials) reads the Kohathite figure in agreement with the MT, and the 8,300 emendation is a scholarly proposal sometimes noted in critical apparatus rather than a manuscript variant. (The Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch broadly preserve the same census numbers as the MT, so the discrepancy is not resolved by an existing version; the 8,300 reading is a reconstruction.) The conjecture is nonetheless attractive because a hundreds-digit slip (300 vs. 600) is exactly the sort of error that arises easily in numeral transmission, where digits and digit-signs are notoriously unstable. George Buchanan Gray's ICC *Numbers* sets out the arithmetic difficulty and the proposed emendation in detail.

This sharpens rather than dissolves the critical picture, and it is not the only critical option. A second view treats the round 22,000 as an independent, possibly schematic total drawn from a different stratum than the itemized clan figures, with the two never fully reconciled — in which case there is nothing to 'emend' because the numbers were never a single arithmetical system. Others simply leave the discrepancy unresolved. Baruch Levine (Anchor Bible) and Jacob Milgrom (JPS) both note that the Priestly census figures do not consistently reconcile and bear the marks of complex transmission; Milgrom discusses the firstborn-substitution scheme and the arithmetic of 3:39-51 in detail. Emanuel Tov's *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* documents precisely this class of phenomenon — mismatches between a rounded grand total and the sum of its components — as a recurrent feature of numerical transmission in the Hebrew Bible, where digits were especially prone to corruption. Whether one judges the MT 8,600 a copyist's slip (with a conjectured original of 8,300) or treats the whole census apparatus as a layered Priestly composition whose round total and itemized subtotals never fully cohered, the result is the same: the discrepancy is a transmission/composition artifact, not a substantive claim about firstborn bookkeeping.

Verdict: most plausibly a scribal/numeral corruption or a composite-total seam. The firstborn-Levite theory is contextually motivated and internally coherent, and one cannot strictly rule it out — but it depends on an unstated qualification of 3:39 and a stipulated figure of 300. A single hundreds-digit corruption in the Kohathite total (8,600 for an original 8,300) yields a consistent 22,000 and is the simpler account, even though it rests on conjecture rather than an attested version.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The discrepancy plausibly reflects a hundreds-digit numeral corruption — a commonly proposed text-critical explanation conjectures an original Kohathite total of 8,300 (rather than the MT's 8,600), which would make the three subtotals sum to exactly 22,000 and match Numbers 3:39, a recognized class of transmission error. The apologetic firstborn-deduction theory is internally coherent but requires reading an unstated qualification into 3:39 and a stipulated figure of 300; no attested Septuagint variant securely supplies the 8,300 reading.

entries.question: How many generations must a bastard wait until his offspring can enter the congregation of the Lord?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 23:2 bars the offspring of an illegitimate union from the assembly of YHWH for ten generations, but the genealogies of David in Matthew 1 and Luke 3 trace him back through Pharez (the son of Judah and Tamar's incestuous union) in only nine generations. The legal rule and the messianic genealogy don't line up.
entries.commentary:
Deuteronomy 23:2 is unambiguous in the Hebrew. The word *mamzer* gets translated "bastard" in the KJV, and the verse says no *mamzer* shall enter the congregation of YHWH "even to his tenth generation." Most lexicons (HALOT, BDB) treat *mamzer* as offspring of a forbidden union — the rabbinic tradition (m. Yebamot 4:13) narrowed it to incest and adultery, but the older Deuteronomic stratum reads as a blanket exclusion of illegitimate children and their descendants for ten generations. Genesis 38 then hands us Pharez, born to Judah from his daughter-in-law Tamar — exactly the kind of forbidden union that would qualify under any reasonable reading of *mamzer*. Matthew 1:3-5 and Luke 3:31-33 both run David's line through Pharez and count nine generations, not ten.

The apologetic harmonization runs in three directions. First, narrow the definition: Gleason Archer in his *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* argues *mamzer* technically means "child of a mixed-cult marriage" or "offspring of a Canaanite cultic prostitute," not any illegitimate child. Second, dismiss the genealogy as schematic: Matthew is famously stylized into 14-14-14, so the apologist says you can't count generations literally. Third, claim the law applies only after Sinai, so Pharez was grandfathered in. Take your pick.

None of these hold up well. The narrow-cult-prostitute reading isn't supported by the Hebrew or by the rabbinic interpretation in m. Yebamot, which understood *mamzer* to cover incest cases like Tamar's. The schematic-genealogy defense actually concedes the contradiction by admitting Matthew's count isn't reliable, which then opens up bigger problems for using these genealogies to establish Davidic descent at all. And the "law applied later" move ignores that the Deuteronomist is presenting these laws as binding from Sinai forward — yet Boaz, David, and Solomon are all later than Sinai in the biblical chronology and are still inside the ten generations from Pharez. The plain reading of the Deuteronomic law and the plain reading of the messianic genealogy are in tension.

The critical-scholarly response is the more parsimonious one. The genealogies in Matthew and Luke were composed centuries after the Deuteronomic Code crystallized, and the authors were not running the math against Deuteronomy 23. Critical scholars (Christine Hayes on Second Temple intermarriage halakhah, Jeffrey Tigay in his JPS Deuteronomy commentary) note that Deuteronomy 23 reflects an ideology of exclusionary purity that later Second Temple texts (Ezra-Nehemiah) intensified, while the Davidic genealogy preserves an older inclusive tradition that simply didn't engage with the Deuteronomic exclusion. The contradiction is what you get when two streams of tradition get bound into the same canon without anyone reconciling them.

- Jeffrey H. Tigay, *Deuteronomy* (JPS Torah Commentary, Jewish Publication Society, 1996).
- Christine E. Hayes, *Gentile Impurities and Jewish Identities: Intermarriage and Conversion from the Bible to the Talmud* (Oxford University Press, 2002).
- Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).
- Raymond E. Brown, *The Birth of the Messiah* (Anchor Bible Reference Library, Doubleday, updated ed. 1993).

Phares ... [Phares was a "bastard" to God. (See Genesis 38:)]

commentary_out.commentary:
Deuteronomy 23:2 (MT 23:3) is unambiguous in the Hebrew: "No *mamzer* (מַמְזֵר) shall enter the assembly of YHWH; even to the tenth generation none of his shall enter the assembly of YHWH." The KJV "bastard" captures the gist but flattens a famously obscure word. *Mamzer* appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible (here and Zechariah 9:6), and its etymology is contested; HALOT and BDB register it as the offspring of an illicit union without pinning down the precise prohibited category. The Septuagint of Deuteronomy 23:3 (LXX numbering) renders the clause ἐκ πόρνης ("born of a prostitute") — a free, interpretive rendering rather than a strict lexical equivalent — and the Vulgate has *de scorto natus*; both are already interpretive guesses about a word the translators no longer securely understood. The Tannaitic tradition (m. Yebamot 4:13) narrowed *mamzer* to the issue of unions punishable by *karet* or death — chiefly incest and adultery — but the older Deuteronomic stratum reads as a blanket multi-generational exclusion. The phrase "to the tenth generation" stands in close parallel to the very next verses (Deut 23:3-4 MT 23:4-5), where the exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites is glossed *ad olam* ("forever"); on that reading "tenth generation" functions as an idiom for perpetuity rather than a literal countdown, which sharpens the problem rather than softening it.

Genesis 38 then hands us Perez (Pharez), born to Judah by his daughter-in-law Tamar — a union the narrator frames as both deceptive and incestuous (Lev 18:15 explicitly bars a man from his daughter-in-law). Under the rabbinic incest definition of *mamzer*, Perez is a textbook case. Matthew 1:3-6 and Luke 3:31-33 both route David's line through Perez. The arithmetic must be stated carefully. Perez is the *mamzer* — generation zero, the disqualified ancestor. His descendants run Hezron, Ram (Aram), Amminadab, Nahshon (Naasson), Salmon, Boaz (Booz), Obed, Jesse, David. Counting only Perez's descendants, David is the *ninth* in line; counting names inclusive of Perez himself, David is the tenth name in the list. The contradiction depends on the first count: David, the messianic fountainhead, enters the assembly as the ninth generation issuing from the *mamzer* Perez — one short of the tenth-generation bar that would clear his line. (Listing ten names is not the same as nine generations of descendants; Perez is excluded from the count of those barred-then-cleared, since he is the *mamzer* himself, not one of his ten generations of descendants.)

The apologetic harmonization runs three ways. First, narrow the definition: Gleason Archer's *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* restricts *mamzer* to the child of cultic prostitution or mixed-cult marriage, not ordinary illegitimacy. Second, dismiss the count as schematic: Matthew's genealogy is openly stylized into three sets of fourteen (Matt 1:17), telescoping generations, so it cannot be pressed arithmetically — and indeed Matthew demonstrably omits three Davidic kings (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) between Joram and Uzziah in 1:8, so the list is selective by design. Third, the chronological move: the law post-dates Sinai and could not retroactively bind Perez.

Each has weaknesses. The cult-prostitute reading lacks lexical support; the Hebrew gives no such qualifier, and the LXX's "born of a prostitute" is itself a gloss, not a cultic specification. The schematic-genealogy defense is double-edged: conceding that Matthew's count is unreliable undercuts the very genealogical argument used to certify Davidic (and thus messianic) descent, and in any case the law's clock runs from Perez regardless of how many names the evangelist omits — telescoping would only make the qualifying descendant arrive sooner, not later, and Luke's fuller list (Luke 3:31-33) likewise yields nine descendants. The chronological defense ignores that Boaz, Jesse, David, and Solomon all post-date Sinai in the biblical timeline yet fall inside ten generations of Perez; the Deuteronomist presents the law as binding from Sinai forward, and a perpetuity reading ("forever," per the *ad olam* parallel) would bar the line regardless.

The more economical critical read is that the Deuteronomic exclusion and the Davidic genealogy belong to different traditions that were never harmonized. Tigay's JPS commentary notes that Deuteronomy 23 reflects a purity ideology later intensified in Ezra-Nehemiah's campaign against mixed marriage, while the genealogy preserves an older inclusive memory. Christine Hayes situates the *mamzer* rule within evolving Second Temple intermarriage halakhah, where the boundaries of "who may enter" were precisely the contested question. Raymond Brown and Davies-Allison observe that the evangelists' inclusion of Tamar (and Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba) is theologically pointed — flagging irregular unions as part of a deliberate motif, not policing them against Deuteronomy 23. The tension is real but "disputed": whether it counts as a contradiction depends on which reading of *mamzer* one adopts and how literally one presses a genealogy the evangelist openly stylized. Verdict: overstated as bare arithmetic, but genuine as an unreconciled clash of traditions — an exclusionary purity law and an inclusive messianic genealogy bound into one canon without anyone harmonizing the count.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The collision depends on (a) reading *mamzer* broadly enough to cover Tamar's union and (b) pressing Matthew's openly schematic, telescoped genealogy arithmetically; on the narrow rabbinic-cultic definition or the schematic-genealogy reading the numerical contradiction loosens, though the broader clash between Deuteronomy's exclusionary ideology and the genealogy's inclusiveness remains.
